sector: Real Estate / Healthcare - Retirement Villages & Aged Care
overview: Summerset Group Holdings is one of New Zealand's largest retirement village developers and operators, building and managing a portfolio of 44 villages across New Zealand with a nascent but growing presence in Victoria, Australia (4 villages under development). Founded in 1997 and NZX-listed since 2011 (also ASX-listed as SNZ), the company operates under the Occupation Right Agreement (ORA) model: residents pay an upfront licence fee for the right to occupy a unit, and Summerset earns a Deferred Management Fee (DMF) equal to 25% of the original ORA price upon exit. At FY2025 year-end (31 December 2025), total assets were NZ$9.2 billion, the portfolio comprised 8,673 total units, residents numbered 9,500+ and the land bank held 5,499 retirement units plus 1,173 care units across both countries.

business_model.summary: Capital-intensive ORA/DMF model where reported operating cash flow (OCF) is materially inflated by ORA receipts from residents — these are economically a financing flow (residents' loans of $3.3b on the balance sheet), not free cash flow. Management's preferred earnings measure is Underlying Profit, which strips out IFRS fair-value property revaluations and reinstates only realised development margins and resale gains. Revenue is predominantly recurring (care fees/village services ~62%, DMF income ~37%) but earnings quality depends heavily on: (1) new unit sales generating development margin, (2) resale activity generating resale gains, and (3) NZ residential property market conditions, which drive ORA pricing and resale velocity.

revenue_streams.name: Care fees and village services
revenue_streams.notes: FY25: $223.6m, up 13% YoY. Includes care fees paid by residents and Health NZ ($55.7m in FY25), plus village weekly fees. Growing with portfolio size and care ORA conversion.

revenue_streams.name: Deferred management fees (DMF)
revenue_streams.notes: FY25: $137.2m, up 13% YoY. Earned on exit at 25% of original ORA price over 5 years. Growing as portfolio matures and resale volumes increase.

business_model.ocf_note: Reported OCF of $548.2m in FY25 includes $746.6m of ORA receipts from new sales and resales, net of $220.4m repayments to departing residents. These net ORA flows ($526.2m) are residents' loans — a liability on the balance sheet — not income. True underlying operational cash generation is better proxied by Underlying Profit ($234.2m). CapEx was $722.4m in FY25, resulting in a net investment outflow of $174.2m (OCF minus CapEx) that is funded by debt.
business_model.customer_type: B2C — primarily retirees aged 70+ seeking independent living with continuum-of-care access. Health NZ (Te Whatu Ora) is a significant care fee payer ($55.7m in FY25, ~25% of care fee revenue).
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~94% of units delivered in FY25 (637 of 693). Portfolio spans 40 NZ villages across 11 regions, with no single region >20% of resales. Australia ~6% of FY25 deliveries (56 units). Four Victorian sites: Cranbourne North (open, care commencing FY26), Chirnside Park (open), Oakleigh South (under construction, FY27 deliveries), Torquay (under construction, FY27 deliveries).

main_competitors: Ryman Healthcare (RYM.NZ) — historically the largest NZ operator (~49 villages NZ/Australia) but severely financially stressed; completed two major equity raises totalling ~$2b in 2023-2025 and largely paused new development. Completed a $150m secured bond raise in June 2026. Continuing operational recovery mode.
Metlifecare — private NZ operator (~35 villages), taken private by EQT in 2021. No longer a listed competitor but a significant operational competitor for residents.
Oceania Healthcare (OCA.NZ) — listed NZX, care-heavy model. Smaller than Summerset, faces similar funding pressures.
Arvida Group (ARV.NZ) — formerly listed NZX, taken private by US infrastructure fund Stonepeak in 2024. Growth model focused on acquisitions; no longer a direct listed peer.
Bupa Care Services NZ — large private aged care and retirement village operator.
RetireAustralia / Lendlease / Aveo — major Australian operators in Summerset's target Victorian market.
competitive_position.market_position: One of the 'big two' actively growing listed NZ retirement village operators (the other being Oceania). Summerset claims the largest and most diverse land bank in the NZ retirement village sector. Leads NZ market on brand 'consideration' and 'first choice' metrics per internal surveys. Care centre occupancy 94% vs ~90% industry average. 91% village and 89% care resident satisfaction (FY25).

moat_factors.description: 5,499-unit retirement land bank plus 1,173 care units across NZ and Australia — the largest in the NZ sector by management's claim. This multi-decade pipeline took years and significant capital to assemble and is not easily replicated by competitors. Includes consented sites across 11 NZ regions and 4 Victorian locations.

moat_factors.factor: Broadacre development model and in-house capability
moat_factors.description: Fully integrated in-house capability: land acquisition, planning, consenting, design, procurement and construction management. This enables: (a) cost discipline — FY25 development margin 27.8%, well above the 20-25% medium-term guidance; (b) flexible build rate — Summerset can ramp up or down within quarters based on market conditions; (c) award-winning procurement (CIPS Australasia Best Procurement Transformation, 2025). Contrasts with Ryman, which has historically outsourced more and suffered cost overruns.

91% village and 89% care resident satisfaction (4-5 out of 5 scale). Village NPS of 55, care NPS of 46. Seven consecutive years as Highly Commended Trusted Brand (Reader's Digest). Named Customer Champion by Australian Financial Review (2025). Staff retention 84% (well above sector average), eNPS 51 (top 5% of NZ healthcare providers). These metrics reinforce demand, pricing power, and care quality differentiation.

Residents make a significant capital commitment (average new ORA $693k) and face emotional and practical barriers to moving. DMF accrues at 5%/year, capped at 25% after 5 years, incentivising longer stays. The model is capital-efficient for growth — ORA receipts from new residents partially fund construction of the next units.

44 NZ villages across 11 regions provides resilience to local property market weakness. Only 43% of FY25 resales came from Auckland/Wellington/Christchurch. Active in 22 locations across NZ and Australia. This allows prudent management of build rates by region and limits concentration risk.

Residents can move from independent living into care within the same village. Care ORA conversion programme significantly improved Care EBITDA from $2.7m (FY24) to $18.8m (FY25). Target of $20-25k care EBITDA per bed medium-term vs current ~$13k. First Australian continuum-of-care offering launching at Cranbourne North in FY26.

weaknesses: High and rising debt ($1.97b at FY25 year-end vs $1.71b at FY24 year-end) requires disciplined management; approaching the $2.0b lower end of the $2.0-2.5b target band
Care business remains structurally underpowered: government funding increases consistently lag wage and operational cost inflation, particularly for nursing staff
Australian operations are pre-revenue and pre-scale — execution risk is high and the opportunity to create value is front-end loaded with cost and risk

Ryman's financial distress (though a competitive risk in the medium term) has reduced competitive intensity in NZ — a recovering Ryman with a restructured balance sheet could intensify competition for new sites and residents from 2027 onwards

ORA model concentrates revenue risk in a single NZ property market — a sustained downturn in NZ house prices compresses development margins, slows resale velocity, and reduces fair value investment property gains

growth_drivers: Demographic tailwind — the most powerful structural driver: NZ population aged 75+ is expected to double by 2048 and nearly triple over 50 years. Victoria, Australia's over-75 population expected to grow from ~550,000 today to ~1.2m over 40 years. Sector supply is structurally short of demand; NZ estimated to need 13,000 new aged care beds, with retirement villages expected to provide ~5,000.

Australia expansion gaining real momentum: Cranbourne North village centre (first Australian continuum-of-care facility) delivered December 2025 and commencing aged care operations FY26. Chirnside Park villas 60% pre-sold on first release. Oakleigh South and Torquay under construction. Targeting ~300 units/year Australia by end of FY27. Planning permit lodged for fifth site (Mornington, Victoria). If Summerset replicates its NZ model, Australia effectively doubles the total addressable market.

Care ORA conversion programme: converting standard care beds to ORA arrangements is significantly improving care profitability. Care EBITDA surged from $2.7m (FY24) to $18.8m (FY25); 767 further care units identified for conversion. Medium-term target of $20-25k care EBITDA per bed vs current ~$13k.

Portfolio maturation and compounding resale gains: as the portfolio grows and ages, resale volumes increase organically without requiring additional capital deployment. FY25: 755 resales (+16% YoY) generating $104.5m in realised gains across 32 villages. 10 villages achieved 30+ resales. Average resale proceeds $582k. Embedded value of $1.9b represents future cash when units turn over.

Land bank monetisation with deferred acquisition cost: 5,499-unit NZ and Australia land bank acquired at historic cost provides growth runway to almost double portfolio size. FY26 NZ build guidance of 650-700 homes. Consenting programme progressing — resource consents received for Rotorua, Mosgiel, Belmont (Auckland). New village extension approved at Waikanae on previously earmarked divestment land.

Interest rate normalisation tailwinds: RBNZ has cut the OCR significantly from its 2024 peak. Lower rates reduce finance costs on $1.97b debt, improve NZ property market conditions (supporting higher ORA pricing and resale velocity), and expand investment property valuations (supporting NTA growth). Summerset is operationally leveraged to a falling rate environment.

Technology and operational efficiency investments: Lumin resident platform rolling out to all 39 villages in FY26, remote National Clinical Support (NCS) nursing service expanding to all NZ care centres, AI transcription and care-insight tools piloted, robotic lawnmowers (33 units across 5 villages) and vacuum cleaners (76 units across 22 village centres) deployed — compounding efficiency improvements that reduce cost per resident over time.

business.risk: NZ residential property market downturn reducing ORA pricing and resale velocity
business.description: Summerset's DMF income, development margin, NTA and IFRS earnings are all linked to NZ residential property values. A prolonged property downturn reduces ORA prices, slows resale turnover (fewer retirees can sell existing homes to fund ORAs), compresses development margins, and reduces investment property fair value gains. The NZ market was subdued through 2022-2025 and only beginning to show recovery signs. Despite this, Summerset delivered record sales in FY25, demonstrating resilience, but a sharper or prolonged downturn could materially impact all key financial metrics.

business.risk: Uncontracted stock accumulation and slow sell-down
business.description: As at FY25 year-end, 541 new units and 208 resale units were available for sale (9.7% of portfolio). Metro Auckland (St Johns, Half Moon Bay) and Wellington (Boulcott) villages have above-normal apartment stock to sell through. Management is focused on sell-down ahead of FY26 village centre deliveries. H1 2025 data showed good progress — uncontracted villa stock down 53% — but any acceleration in apartment deliveries without matching sales pace would increase uncontracted stock further.

Government funding rates (Health NZ) for residential care consistently increase below actual wage and operational cost inflation, particularly for nursing staff. Care EBITDA per bed in completed villages is ~$13k vs the $20-25k medium-term target. Operating expenses grew 16% in FY25 driven largely by healthcare wage costs. An Aged Care Advisory Group was formed in October 2025 and is expected to report to government in June 2026. Outcomes and timing of any meaningful reform are highly uncertain.

business.risk: Construction cost inflation and development margin compression
business.description: FY25 development margin of 27.8% was above the 20-25% medium-term guidance range due to a favourable villa-heavy mix. Management has guided for margins to track back toward 20-25% as more care centres and apartment suites settle in FY26, which carry lower margins. Sustained cost inflation could erode margins further if ORA pricing does not keep pace.

financial.risk: Interest-bearing debt approaching target band ceiling
financial.description: Interest-bearing debt of $1,971m at FY25 year-end (up from $1,714m at FY24) represents 21% of total assets and is approaching the $2.0b lower end of management's $2.0-2.5b target debt band. Finance costs were $32m in FY25 (up from $26m in FY24, +22%). Gearing ratio 37.1%, within the 30-40% target band but leaving limited headroom. Management expects aggregate net debt growth to reduce in FY26 as fewer large village centre commercial builds are active. However, Australian expansion will continue to require capital investment before generating meaningful cash flows.

financial.risk: OCF inflation masking true cash generation
financial.description: Reported operating cash flow of $548.2m in FY25 is meaningfully inflated by net ORA inflows (~$526m) which represent residents' loans on the balance sheet, not free cash flow. True operational cash generation is better proxied by Underlying Profit ($234.2m). With CapEx of $722.4m in FY25, the business consumed significantly more cash than it generated operationally, with the gap funded by net new borrowings. Investors reading OCF alone will materially overestimate underlying earnings power.

Growing Australian operations create NZD/AUD translation exposure. A weaker AUD reduces the NZD value of Australian assets and any eventual earnings. In H1 2025, an $1.5m gain on translation of foreign currency operations was recorded in other comprehensive income (FY24 full year was a $2.1m loss). Immaterial at current Australian scale but will grow as Australia expands.

regulatory.risk: NZ Retirement Villages Act Amendment Bill (expected mid-2026 introduction to Parliament)
regulatory.description: NZ Government announced in December 2025 plans to introduce the Retirement Villages Amendment Bill to Parliament during 2026 (expected by July 2026). Key proposed changes: (1) mandatory cessation of weekly fees immediately after a resident vacates; (2) no charging for operator-owned chattel maintenance; (3) interest payable to outgoing residents after 6 months if their unit remains unsold; (4) mandatory buy-back/repayment within 12 months post-vacate if unsold. Summerset states its practices already substantially align (it already pays interest after 6 months and typically repurchases within 12 months). However, the mandatory buy-back creates liquidity risk in a slow market: if multiple units go unsold past 12 months simultaneously, Summerset may need to fund repayments before collecting ORA receipts from replacements. The Bill applies only to new ORAs signed one year after the Act passes, providing transition time. Smaller operators face greater risk, and systemic pressure on the broader sector could impair the whole market.

regulatory.risk: Australian Aged Care Act compliance and operational readiness
regulatory.description: Australia's new Aged Care Act came into force on 1 November 2025. Summerset is commencing aged care operations at Cranbourne North for the first time in FY26. Any compliance failures, staffing shortfalls, or accreditation delays could halt the Australian care launch, damage the brand at the critical moment of market entry, and delay the path to the Australia 300 units/year target.

regulatory.risk: Aged care sector funding model reform
regulatory.description: The NZ Aged Care Advisory Group formed in October 2025 is expected to report in June 2026. Any positive outcomes (higher care funding, improved subsidy rates) could be a material earnings tailwind. Adverse outcomes or extended delays perpetuate the structural funding gap that caps care profitability. The Care ORA model provides a partial but not complete solution to this structural issue.

macro.risk: Interest rate movements and NZ economic conditions
macro.description: After the RBNZ cut rates significantly from the 5.5% peak in 2023-24, the NZ economic environment is showing early recovery signs entering 2026. Lower interest rates benefit Summerset both directly (lower finance costs on $1.97b debt) and indirectly (improved NZ property market, better retiree ability to sell homes). However, any stalling of the rate-cutting cycle, or a return to elevated rates, would re-tighten both channels simultaneously.

macro.risk: NZ and Australian construction cost and labour inflation
macro.description: Operating expenses grew 16% in FY25 to $328.6m, driven by employee costs (58% of opex), with healthcare wages rising faster than government funding increases. NZ construction and healthcare labour markets remain tight. Summerset partially mitigates through procurement discipline (CIPS award) and standardised designs, but sustained above-CPI labour inflation is a persistent earnings headwind, especially in care operations.

macro.risk: Australian property market and demand execution
macro.description: Summerset is entering the Victorian retirement village market without an established track record. The Australian residential property market has its own cycle and is not correlated with NZ. Melbourne's apartment and property market conditions in 2025-2026 will influence early ORA pricing and sales velocity at Chirnside Park and future sites.

execution.description: Summerset delivered only 56 Australian units in FY25 and has guided for 100-150 in FY26. Reaching ~300/year by end of FY27 from this base requires simultaneous scaling across 4+ sites in an unfamiliar regulatory, labour, and market environment, while launching care operations for the first time in Australia. Hiring, accreditation, supply chain development, brand building, and financial performance all need to come together. Cost overruns or demand shortfalls could impair returns and delay Australia's contribution to group earnings. Management acknowledges transitioning from construction partner model to in-house self-management adds further execution complexity.

execution.risk: Village centre build programme complexity and delivery concentration
execution.description: FY25 had the highest ever number of simultaneous commercial builds (12 projects active in NZ). Five more NZ village centre buildings are due in FY26 (Whangārei, Waikanae, Milldale, Prebbleton, Blenheim), plus the Cambridge and Cranbourne North openings. Village centres contain care centres, serviced apartments and amenities — more complex and lower-margin than villas. Any delivery delays or cost overruns would impact FY26 results.

New CFO Margaret Warrington joined February 2025. Chief Sales Officer Fay French stepped back from ELT due to health (remains in the business); Chief Marketing Officer Kay Brodie planning to retire in 2026. These roles are being consolidated into a single new Chief Sales and Marketing Officer role, with David Martin (formerly Metlifecare) joining as transformation lead in January 2026. Senior leadership changes during an expansion phase carry transition risk, particularly as Australia requires brand-building effort.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ retirement village sector has strong secular demand tailwinds: the over-75 population is set to double by 2048. Industry supply has historically been insufficient to meet demand growth (NZ estimated to need ~13,000 additional aged care beds, with retirement villages providing ~5,000). As of mid-2026, NZ property market is showing early recovery signs following a prolonged downturn, supported by RBNZ rate cuts. Sector-wide competitive intensity reduced as Ryman paused development and Arvida went private. Australia (Victoria specifically) is a large greenfield opportunity with lower retirement village penetration rates than NZ, supported by Victoria's over-75 population doubling over 40 years. The sector is structurally sound but continues to face government care funding inadequacy that constrains profitability of the care business.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high cyclicality tied to residential property market. Business fundamentals (DMF, care fees) are relatively stable and provide a floor. But development margins, NTA growth, and new sales velocity are all correlated with property prices and buyer confidence. Resale activity is also linked to general property market liquidity. The demographic demand floor is strong but does not prevent cyclical swings in timing and velocity of sales.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — dual sensitivity: (1) Rising rates increase finance costs on $1.97b debt directly (every 100bps shift on floating portion is ~$10-15m p.a.); (2) Higher rates reduce NZ property market activity, slowing ORA sales as retirees struggle to sell existing homes. RBNZ rate cuts through 2024-2025 are a meaningful tailwind. Management expects gearing to decline as the portfolio matures and Australia passes its peak capex phase.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Limited but growing AUD/NZD exposure as Australian operations scale. All reporting in NZD. Currently immaterial (~6% of deliveries in Australia) but will grow to ~25-30% of deliveries by end of FY27 on management targets.
key_input_costs: Healthcare labour (nurses, caregivers) — largest operating cost at 58% of opex ($190.6m in FY25); exposed to minimum wage and sector wage inflation well above the level of government funding increases
Construction materials (concrete, steel, timber) — standardised designs, EC30 reduced-carbon concrete standard, and mature procurement programmes partially mitigate inflation
Insurance and council rates — both increasing above CPI; property-related expenses $33.6m in FY25 (10% of opex)
Energy costs — accelerating transition to solar (1,500+ panels added in FY25) and away from gas (28 villages to convert off gas by 2028) to reduce exposure

recent_developments.event: H1-2026 result (six months to 30 June 2026). Underlying profit $103.4m, DOWN 3.0% on H1-2025's $106.6m -- the first half-on-half decline in the series. Statutory NPAT of $171.4m (+91.7%) is not comparable: it reflects a $191.1m investment-property fair value movement against a restated base. Revenue $200.3m (+15.7%). Total ORA sales 813 units (398 new, 415 resales). Retirement units in portfolio 7,458; care units 1,696. Interim dividend 3.8cps. NTA $14.41/share.

PRIOR-PERIOD RESTATEMENT disclosed in Note 1 of the H1-2026 interim report -- two corrections of error. (a) Investment property fair value did not correctly account for loans to residents under NZ IAS 40, overstating investment property and fair value gains. (b) The timing of derecognition of residents' loans for transferring residents changed. Restated comparatives: H1-2025 NPAT $127.2m -> $89.4m, equity $3,173.5m -> $3,110.8m, NTA 1318.44c -> 1292c; FY2025 total assets $9,234.9m -> $9,294.2m. No effect on cash flows, banking covenants, revenue or underlying profit.

FY26 GUIDANCE CUT on build rate. NZ deliveries now 600-650 homes (previously 650-700) and total 700-800 (previously 750-850); medium-term group build rate held at 600-700 p.a. Management explicitly flags that lower sales rates in April and early May, in reaction to the Iran fuel crisis, mean Q3-2026 settlements are currently forecast DOWN on prior periods -- described as an isolated quarter with no expected flow-on to Q4. Cash flow from existing operations guided $50-70m (FY25: $32.3m). Construction capex $375-425m. Development margin 20-25%, in line with medium-term guidance.

Balance sheet: net debt $2,058m at 1H26, UP from $1,960m at FY25 despite the deleveraging target, driven by $85.3m development outflow and ~$25m AUD FX translation. Gearing 36.9% against a 30-40% band; company targets 33% and net debt below $1.9b by end-2027. Target debt range REDUCED to $1.75b-$2.25b (previously $2.0b-$2.5b). Corporate overhead cost per unit down 6% since FY25.

Operating metrics held up: village resident satisfaction 91% (every village at or above the 80% target, 24 villages above 90%), care satisfaction 88% with all care centres at a positive NPS. Occupancy lifting in new villages; retirement village occupancy target 95%.

Aged Care Advisory Group established by NZ government in October 2025 expected to report to government in June 2026 on a more sustainable aged care funding model. Outcome could materially improve care profitability if positive funding reforms result. Separately, the NZ Retirement Villages Amendment Bill (mandatory 12-month buy-back, interest after 6 months on unsold units, cessation of weekly fees post-vacate) remains on track for introduction to Parliament by July 2026 per government timeline.

Summerset Annual General Meeting held online only on 21 April 2026 (originally planned in-person at Wellington) due to Wellington state of emergency following extreme rainfall and flash flooding. No significant governance or strategic changes announced at AGM.

Final FY2025 dividend of 13.2 cents per share paid on 26 March 2026 (record date 12 March 2026). Full year FY25 dividend of 24.5 cps, flat on FY24, represents 25.3% of underlying profit. Board formally adopted three-year review cycle for dividend policy; policy to be reviewed during FY26.

FY2025 full year results released (27 February 2026): Record underlying profit $234.2m (+13% on FY24), record 1,560 ORA sales (+26% on FY24), 693 units delivered (637 NZ + 56 Australia), NTA $13.75/share (+$1.32 YoY), total assets $9.2b (+15%). IFRS net profit $259.7m (down 22% on FY24 due to lower fair value movements vs prior year). Total debt $1.97b (vs $2.0-2.5b target band).

David Martin joined as Chief Sales and Marketing Transformation Lead, consolidating previously separate sales and marketing ELT roles. Martin brings experience from Metlifecare, where he led the commercial transformation and rebrand. New Golf NZ partnership commenced (naming rights of Charles Tour, plus Pro-Am resident experiences).

NZ Government announced plans to amend the Retirement Villages Act in 2026, including mandatory 12-month buy-back and cessation of weekly fees post-vacate. Summerset states practices already largely align. Village centre building at Cranbourne North (first Australian continuum-of-care facility) completed. First villas at Chirnside Park (second Australian village) delivered — 60% of 28 released homes pre-sold. Construction commenced at Oakleigh South (fourth Australian village). 120 new apartments delivered at St Johns Stage 2.
Australia's new Aged Care Act came into force on 1 November 2025. Summerset working to meet requirements; first Australian aged care operations planned for Cranbourne North in Q2 FY26.

Sod-turning event at Oakleigh South (fourth Australian village). Named a Customer Champion by Australian Financial Review. NZ government formed Aged Care Advisory Group to advise on sustainable funding model, expected to report June 2026.

Record H1 2025 results announced (27 August 2025): underlying profit $106.6m (+19% on H1 2024), IFRS net profit $127.2m (+26%), 692 ORA sales (record first half, +18% on H1 2024), OCF $228.7m (+19%), total assets $8.7b (+18% on H1 2024). Interim dividend 11.3 cps declared. First residents moved into Summerset Rangiora (fifth Canterbury village). No core debt; gearing 36.7%, within target band.

Summerset St Johns received Excellence award at NZ Property Council Awards (Retirement Living and Aged Care category). Record first half results announced. CIPS Australasia Best Procurement Transformation award won by Summerset's construction procurement team.
Margaret Warrington joined as new Chief Financial Officer. Care centre at Summerset Boulcott (Lower Hutt) opened.

guidance.as_of: H1-2026 result and investor presentation, released 2026-08-28

items.notes: Previously guided 650-700. Group medium-term build rate held at 600-700 p.a.
Unchanged from prior guidance; FY25 Australia delivery was 56 homes.
H1-2026 realised unit development margin 20%, at the bottom of the range.
Overhead cost per unit down 6% since FY25.
Previously $2.0b-$2.5b. Targets gearing 33% and net debt below $1.9b by end-2027.

guidance.caveat: Q3-2026 settlements are guided DOWN on prior periods following weak April/early-May sales rates attributed to the Iran fuel crisis. Management calls this an isolated quarter. Weekly sales rates for Q3 are said to be tracking ahead of the first two quarters of 2026.

bull_case: Demographic demand is the most powerful structural growth driver in the NZ-listed universe: NZ's 75+ population doubles by 2048 while sector supply structurally undershoots demand. Summerset's 5,499-unit land bank pipeline was assembled at historical cost and provides a multi-decade delivery runway at minimal incremental land cost. This is a near-irreplaceable competitive asset.

Australia is now genuinely executing, not just planning: Cranbourne North village centre delivered, Chirnside Park first homes 60% pre-sold on launch, Oakleigh South and Torquay under construction, Mornington permit lodged. If Summerset replicates even a fraction of its NZ model success in Victoria — where retirement village penetration is lower and the market is larger — the long-run earnings power is substantially underpriced at current NTA-based valuations. Early brand reception (AFR Customer Champion award) is encouraging.

Resale gains are a compounding, capital-light flywheel: 755 resales in FY25 generating $104.5m in realised gains. As 32 villages already generating resales, and with embedded portfolio value of $1.9b representing future cash on unit turnover, this stream grows organically with portfolio maturation without requiring further land or build investment. The resale earnings flywheel spins faster every year.

Interest rate normalisation is a multi-year tailwind: RBNZ rate cuts reduce Summerset's own finance costs (on $1.97b debt), improve NZ property market conditions (lifting ORA pricing and retiree ability to fund a move), and expand NTA valuations. Summerset's balance sheet discipline — no core debt, gearing within target band — means it is well positioned to benefit from improving conditions unlike Ryman, which has been forced into capital raises.

Competitive landscape is structurally more favourable than at any time in the last decade: Ryman paused development after two massive capital raises totalling ~$2b. Arvida went private and removed from the NZX competitive field. Metlifecare remains private. Summerset is the dominant actively building, NZX-listed retirement village company in NZ, absorbing demand that competitors cannot capture. This window of reduced competition will persist while Ryman works through its balance sheet recovery.
bear_case: Interest-bearing debt of $1.97b is at the floor of the $2.0-2.5b target band, leaving minimal balance sheet headroom. Any unexpected stress — prolonged NZ property downturn, major construction cost blowout, Australian demand shortfall, or regulatory capital requirements from the buy-back legislation — could require dilutive equity issuance or a painful forced reduction in build rates. The business has no margin for error.

OCF is a misleading metric: reported OCF of $548m wildly overstates true cash generation because it includes ~$526m of net ORA inflows, which are residents' loans (a financial liability). Underlying Profit of $234m is the relevant earnings proxy, and with CapEx of $722m, Summerset consumed $488m more cash than it earned operationally in FY25, funded entirely by debt. This is not a cash-generative business at the current build scale.

Australian execution risk is high and the opportunity is back-end loaded: Summerset delivered just 56 Australian units in FY25. Reaching 300/year by end of FY27 (a 5x increase in 2 years) while simultaneously launching aged care, building brand, managing 4+ simultaneous construction sites, and transitioning to self-managed construction across an unfamiliar market is ambitious. Any delay pushes the Australia profitability timeline materially, while capital continues to be deployed.

The NZ Retirement Villages Amendment Bill introduces the mandatory 12-month buy-back obligation. While Summerset says its practices already align, legislating the obligation changes the risk profile for a slow market: if multiple units go unsold past 12 months simultaneously, Summerset must fund repayments before new ORA receipts arrive, creating liquidity pressure. More concerning is the systemic risk — smaller operators who cannot absorb this obligation may exit the market, reducing supply capacity and potentially creating adverse media coverage that deters residents across the whole sector.

IFRS earnings are inherently volatile and confusing to investors: FY25 IFRS net profit was $259.7m, down 22% from $332m in FY24, despite underlying profit growing 13%. The difference is entirely driven by the fair value movement of investment properties, which itself is driven by external property valuers' assumptions about NZ house prices and growth rates. If NZ property recovery stalls or reverses, fair value gains turn to losses, IFRS earnings become negative headlines, and investors who do not understand the underlying model sell — potentially disconnecting price from intrinsic value. This creates meaningful stock volatility risk.
analysis_note_2026_08_28: Narrative refreshed on the H1-2026 result. The headline to carry into any valuation: underlying profit -- the measure this business is valued on -- went BACKWARDS 3.0%, while statutory NPAT nearly doubled on a fair-value movement against a restated base. Anyone reading the +91.7% NPAT line as growth is reading an accounting artefact. Build guidance was cut and Q3 settlements are pre-warned lower.
